name: Cold start cost of loading a model makes reactive autoscaling structurally late
symptom: New replicas take 2-10 minutes to start because multi-gigabyte weights must load from storage. By the time the new replica is ready, the traffic spike has passed. The fleet is always either over-provisioned (wasting money) or under-provisioning (dropping SLOs).
root_cause: LLM models are large (10-100+ GB). Loading weights from disk/network takes minutes. Kubernetes HPA reacts to current load, but by the time new pods are scheduled, pulled, and loaded, the load spike has passed. This is a structural problem: no amount of reaction speed can beat the actuation delay. The 2026 paper 'Decomposing Predictive Kubernetes Autoscaling for Large Language Model Serving Under Long Startup Delays' (arXiv:2609.20874) shows that reactive QPS-based scaling has 53% TTFT SLO violations, while predictive scaling with startup-delay lookahead reduces this to 0.5%.
workaround: Use predictive autoscaling: forecast load and start replicas before the spike. KServe with KEDA supports idleReplicaCount=0 for scale-to-zero, but this requires predictive scaling to work. Pre-warm replicas during known peak hours. Use model caching (KServe LocalModel, OCI model delivery) to reduce load time. Consider smaller models or LoRA adapters that load faster.
notes: This is the fundamental tension in LLM autoscaling: models are too large to load quickly, but traffic is too spiky to pre-provision. The solution is predictive scaling - forecasting load and starting replicas before the spike. The arXiv paper shows that a simple EWMA with delay-aware lookahead captures most of the benefit, and that Kalman filters do NOT consistently beat EWMA (a useful negative result). KServe v0.21.0's KEDA integration with idleReplicaCount=0 is the first production-ready scale-to-zero path, but it requires predictive scaling to be useful.
